                                  25   Panacea as the exclusive financial services company to establish and maintain an affinity program

                                  26   for ADA members for various financial services products and services.” Id. ¶ 19. As a result of

                                  13   ADA in a rudimentary pricing model it shared with Panacea.” Id. ¶ 77.

                                  14          On February 21, 2025, Panacea informed Tallied that Panacea had discovered Tallied’s

                                  15   wrongful actions and that “unless the matter could be amicably resolved, Panacea would have no

                                  18          On April 9, 2025, Panacea filed this lawsuit asserting claims for: (1) breach of contract; (2)

                                  19   unjust enrichment; (3) violation of the Delaware Uniform Trade Secrets Act (“DUTSA”); (4)

                                  20   common law misappropriation/conversion of confidential information; (5) tortious interference

                                  21   with prospective business relationships; and (6) unfair competition.

                                  22   II.    JURISDICTION

                                  23          Panacea alleges that this Court has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1).

                                  24   III.   LEGAL STANDARD

                                  25          A complaint must contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the

                                  26   pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2). “Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) is

                                  27   appropriate only where the complaint lacks a cognizable legal theory or sufficient facts to support

                                  28   a cognizable legal theory.” Mendiondo v. Centinela Hosp. Med. Ctr., 521 F.3d 1097, 1104 (9th
                                                                                         4
                                         Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST            Document 38           Filed 09/24/25     Page 5 of 14




                                   1   Cir. 2008). A complaint need not contain detailed factual allegations, but facts pleaded by a

                                   2   plaintiff “must be enough to raise a right to relief above the speculative level.” Bell Atl. Corp. v.

                                   3   Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain

                                   4   sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”

                                   5   Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). “A

                                   6   claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw

                                   7   the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Id. The Court

                                   8   must “accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light

                                   9   most favorable to the nonmoving party.” Knievel, 393 F.3d at 1072. However, the Court is not

                                  10   “required to accept as true allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact,

                                  11   or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir. 2008)

                                  12   (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).

                                  13   IV.     DISCUSSION

                                  14           A.      DUTSA Claim

                                  15           To state a claim for trade secret misappropriation under the DUTSA, a plaintiff must show

                                  16   that (1) a trade secret exists; (2) the trade secret was acquired by the defendant from the plaintiff;

                                  17   (3) the acquisition was pursuant to an express or implied understanding that the secrecy of the

                                  18   matter would be respected; and (4) the defendant has improperly used or disclosed the secret

                                  19   information to the injury of the plaintiff. See Accenture Glob. Servs. GMBH v. Guidewire

                                  20   Software Inc., 581 F. Supp. 2d 654, 662 (D. Del. 2008) (citing Savor, Inc. v. FMR Corp., No. Civ.

                                  21   A. 10–249, 2004 WL 1965869, *5 (Del. Super. July 15, 2004)).

                                  22           Tallied primarily contests the first and fourth elements—arguing that Panacea “fails to (1)

                                  23   identify the specific material alleged to constitute trade secrets, and (2) allege that Tallied

                                  24   misappropriated or used its trade secrets in connection with the ADA RFP.” ECF No. 28 at 11.

                                  25                   1.      Existence of Trade Secret

                                  26           DUTSA defines a “trade secret” as “information” that:

                                  27                   a. derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not
                                                       being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by
                                  28                   proper means by, other persons who can obtain economic value from
                                                                                            5
                                         Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST           Document 38          Filed 09/24/25     Page 6 of 14



                                                      its disclosure or use; and
                                   1
                                                      b. is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances
                                   2                  to maintain its secrecy.
                                   3   6 Del. C. § 2001(4).
                                   4          In other words, to be considered a trade secret, information must: (1) not be generally

                                   5   known or readily ascertainable; (2) derive independent economic value from not being generally

                                   6   known or readily ascertainable; and (3) be subject to reasonable efforts to maintain its secrecy.

                                   7   See Brightstar Corp. v. PCS Wireless, LLC, No. CVN18C10250PRWCCLD, 2019 WL 3714917,

                                   8   at *4 (Del. Super. Ct. Aug. 7, 2019).

                                   9          Panacea alleges that it disclosed confidential, protectable trade secret information to

                                  10   Tallied, including “proprietary information concerning interchange fees and cost of funding;

                                  11   knowledge of the ADA’s preferences on a credit-card portfolio construct’s features as to account

                                  12   integration, credit lines, rewards structure, conversion experience, acquisition strategy and
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   partnership drivers; and timing and knowledge of the ADA’s anticipated RFP process.” ECF No.

                                  14   29 at 20 (citing ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 40-56, 63-67, 73-77). Tallied argues that Panacea’s alleged trade

                                  15   secrets—knowledge of the ADA’s membership and preferences; knowledge of the ADA RFP; and

                                  16   feedback Panacea provided to Tallied about pricing and revenue share—are described with general

                                  17   catchall categories and lack the specificity to allow Tallied to determine whether Panacea

                                  18   possessed a trade secret rather than non-protectible ideas of concepts. ECF No. 28 at 12. After

                                  19   reviewing the parties’ cited authorities, the Court finds that Panacea has alleged sufficient factual

                                  20   detail to plausibly state, at the pleading stage, the existence of trade secrets regarding the

                                  21   confidential information it shared with Tallied.

                                  22          Unlike cases where the plaintiff “has set out its purported trade secrets in broad,

                                  23   categorical terms, more descriptive of the types of information that generally may qualify as

                                  24   protectable trade secrets,” Vendavo, Inc. v. Price f(x) AG, No. 17-CV-06930-RS, 2018 WL

                                  25   1456697, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 23, 2018), Panacea has specifically described the context, timing,

                                  26   import, and type of information that it shared with Tallied and why that information was secret

                                  27   and valuable to draw clear boundaries as to what trade secrets it alleges.

                                  28          First, as to knowledge about the ADA’s preferences and knowledge of the upcoming ADA
                                                                                          6

                                   1   RFP, Panacea alleges that it made deliberate, extensive efforts to gain that information through

                                   3   provide tailored banking, capital, and financing solutions to medical providers. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 15–

                                   4   16. Its business strategy was specifically to gain a competitive edge by “develop[ing] strong

                                   5   relationships and enter[ing] into affinity partnerships with numerous medical trade associations

                                   6   including,” with the ADA in as early as January 2024. Id. ¶ 18. And its partnership agreement

                                   7   with the ADA “appoint[ed] Panacea as the exclusive financial services company to establish and

                                   8   maintain an affinity program for ADA members for various financial services products and

                                   9   services,” allowing Panacea to gain exclusive information about the ADA’s membership,

                                  10   structure, preferences, and upcoming credit-card issuance opportunity. Id. ¶¶ 19, 21, 23. Through

                                  11   the discussions about this potential credit card partnership, “Panacea obtained valuable, non-

                                  12   public, confidential information regarding the projected program scope and some of the ADA’s
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   desired characteristics for the program and a go-forward partner, including as it related to pricing,

                                  14   conversion, timeline, and technological specifications.” Id. ¶ 26.

                                  15          Panacea has thus alleged the type of institutional knowledge on customer preferences and

                                  16   business opportunities—developed through substantial effort and trusted access—that courts have

                                  17   routinely recognized as trade secrets at the motion to dismiss stage. See Navigation Holdings,

                                  18   LLC v. Molavi, 445 F. Supp. 3d 69, 77 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (finding that the plaintiffs adequately

                                  19   described their trade secrets in compiling price information about proven clients that they gathered

                                  20   over the history of their operations spanning years and many hours of research); Xsolla (USA),

                                  21   Inc. v. Aghanim Inc., No. 2:24-CV-02116-ODW (AGRX), 2024 WL 4139615, at *7 (C.D. Cal.

                                  22   Sept. 10, 2024) (finding that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged customer information trade secrets

                                  23   because its complaint described compiling information about established customers, including

                                  25   took years to develop). And contrary to Tallied’s argument that Panacea does not “attempt to

                                  26   explain how this unspecified information about the ADA derives value from not being generally

                                  27   known, especially given the extensive industry expertise Tallied already had,” ECF No. 28 at 13,

                                  28   Panacea has alleged that its success in the competitive bidding process on the ADA RFP depended
                                                                                         7

                                   1   on its unique knowledge of the ADA being kept secret and that Tallied in fact lacked expertise in

                                   3          Similarly, Panacea has alleged that it disclosed trade secrets regarding its proprietary

                                   4   pricing and financial models shared with Tallied under their MNDA. Panacea specifically alleges

                                   5   that it shared with Tallied between March and May 2024: “proposals concerning the ADA’s credit

                                   6   card program construct, rewards structure, acquisition strategy, and partnership drivers” and

                                   8   further contends that in May 2024, Panacea “provided further, confidential, and detailed feedback

                                   9   on Tallied’s pricing model, including as to the economic model on interchange fees that would be

                                  10   required to share with the ADA for its existing credit card portfolio.” Id. ¶ 47. Panacea thus does

                                  11   not allege a vague claim of “pricing information” in the abstract, but a targeted, customized

                                  12   pricing scheme it developed over a year in close collaboration with the ADA. Xsolla (USA), Inc.,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   2024 WL 4139615, at *7 (finding that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged trade secrets relating to

                                  14   pricing because it alleged spending “countless hours developing confidential and proprietary

                                  15   pricing schemes tailored to the needs of the individual video game developers and publishers

                                  16   . . . which took many years and significant effort and testing to develop”).

                                  17                  2.      Misappropriation

                                  18          Tallied primarily argues that Panacea has not plausibly alleged that Tallied

                                  19   misappropriated any of the purported trade secrets and relies only on speculative circumstantial

                                  20   evidence. Tallied cites cases for the proposition that allegations of similarity or rapid development

                                  21   of a competing product or bid—without more—do not plausibly state a claim for misappropriation

                                  22   of underlying trade secrets to create that product or bid. See ECF No. 28 at 17–19 (citing

                                  23   Accenture Glob. Servs. GMBH v. Guidewire Software Inc., 581 F. Supp. 2d 654 (D. Del. 2008);

                                  24   GMH Capital Partners v. Fitts, 2025 WL 950674 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 28, 2025); and Xsolla (USA),

                                  25   Inc., 2024 WL 4139615). While the Court agrees with the general proposition described in these

                                  26   cases, it finds that under the facts as alleged in the complaint, Panacea has plausibly alleged

                                  27   misappropriation.

                                  28          In its complaint, Panacea alleges that (1) Tallied had been representing to Panacea that it
                                                                                         8
                                         Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST          Document 38         Filed 09/24/25    Page 9 of 14




                                   1   still considered Panacea to be its partner in the ADA RFP process while surreptitiously preparing

                                   2   and submitting its own proposal; (2) Tallied was able to win the RFP as the bidder offering the

                                   3   highest percentage revenue share to the ADA, despite not even including a revenue share in the

                                   4   “rudimentary pricing model it shared with Panacea” during their collaborative efforts; and (3)

                                   5   Tallied generally “lacked the knowledge, personnel, expertise, and contacts to bid on or scale a

                                   6   large credit card portfolio” because it had no business card programs. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 42–43, 65,

                                   7   74–78. Taking these circumstances together, Panacea alleges that Tallied must have used the

                                   8   pricing information it obtained from Panacea to undercut Panacea in the bid process. Id. ¶ 77.

                                   9           Panacea has thus alleged the nature of the information Tallied misappropriated and how it

                                  10   did so (incorporating Panacea’s feedback on revenue share and information about the ADA’s

                                  11   preferences into its bid proposal), as well as why circumstances show it was likely that Tallied

                                  12   misappropriated this information—i.e., Tallied’s nondisclosure of its own bid submission and its
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   sudden ability to offer the more competitive revenue share after gaining this exact expertise from

                                  14   Panacea’s confidential feedback. These allegations sufficiently satisfy the misappropriation

                                  15   element of Panacea’s DUTSA claim, particularly at this stage in a trade-secrets case, where “the

                                  16   exact means of knowing what was used is nearly impossible for Plaintiff to know without

                                  17   discovery.” See Applied Biological Lab’ys, Inc. v. Diomics Corp., No. 3:20-CV-2500-AJB-LL,

                                  18   2021 WL 4060531, at *5 (S.D. Cal. Sept. 7, 2021); see also Yeiser Rsch. & Dev. LLC v. Teknor

                                  19   Apex Co., 281 F. Supp. 3d 1021, 1033, 1043–44 (S.D. Cal. 2017) (finding that plaintiff adequately

                                  20   pled misappropriation by alleging that the defendant had no prior experience in the industry,

                                  21   expressed curiosity in the product being developed by the plaintiff, and subsequently developed a

                                  22   similar product); Eastman Chem. Co. v. AlphaPet Inc., No. CIV.A. 09-971-LPS, 2011 WL

                                  23   5402767, at *9 (D. Del. Nov. 4, 2011), report and recommendation adopted, No. CIV.A. 09-971-

                                  24   LPS, 2011 WL 6148637 (D. Del. Dec. 9, 2011) (finding misappropriation to be adequately pled

                                  25   where the plaintiff in the case provided a description of how the defendants gained access to the

                                  26   trade secrets and how the trade secrets were used to develop a competing product).

                                  27          Furthermore, Tallied’s assertion that it could have plausibly learned about the RFP on its

                                  28   own is beside the point. See ECF No. 28 at 16. Setting aside the fact that the Court must draw all
                                                                                        9
                                        Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST           Document 38        Filed 09/24/25       Page 10 of 14




                                   1   inferences in Panacea’s favor, the value of the information about the ADA RFP came from having

                                   2   insider knowledge about what it would entail and what the ADA wanted before the bid process

                                   3   officially began, as this allowed those with that knowledge to tailor and prepare their proposals

                                   4   accordingly. Tallied could thus very well have misappropriated the trade secrets at issue even if it

                                   5   did eventually learn about the ADA RFP on its own.

                                   6          Accordingly, the Court denies Tallied’s motion to dismiss Panacea’s DUTSA claim.

                                   7          B.      DUTSA Preemption

                                   8          Tallied argues that Panacea’s unjust enrichment, unfair competition, tortious interference,

                                   9   and common law misappropriation claims are preempted by DUTSA.

                                  10          Panacea responds by contending that: (1) dismissing these claims on preemption grounds

                                  11   at the motion to dismiss stage would be premature; (2) it can make its common law claims without

                                  12   proving a trade secret claim; (3) and it is allowed to plead arguments in the alternative under Rule
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   8. ECF No. 29 at 17–20.

                                  14          DUTSA’s preemption provision states that the Act “displaces conflicting tort,

                                  15   restitutionary and other law of this State providing civil remedies for misappropriation of a trade

                                  16   secret.” 6 Del. C. § 2007(a). Courts have interpreted this language to mean that DUTSA

                                  17   preempts claims that are “grounded in the same facts which purportedly support the

                                  18   misappropriation of trade secrets claims.” Ethypharm S.A. France v. Bentley Pharms., Inc., 388 F.

                                  19   Supp. 2d 426, 433 (D. Del. 2005) (quoting Savor, Inc. v. FMR Corp., 2001 WL 541484, at *4

                                  20   (Del. Super. Apr. 24, 2001)). A common law claim is “grounded in the same facts” as a trade

                                  21   secret claim if “the same facts are used to establish all the elements of both claims.” Accenture

                                  22   Global Servs. GMBH v. Guidewire Software Inc., 631 F. Supp. 2d 504, 508 (D. Del. 2009) (citing

                                  23   Ethypharm, 388 F. Supp. 2d at 434–35). In other words, “if the success of the common law claim

                                  24   does not depend on the success of the trade secrets claim, that is, if a plaintiff need not prove all

                                  25   the facts underlying the trade secrets claim in order to prove the common law claim, then the

                                  26   common law claim is not ‘grounded in the same facts’ and is not preempted.” Id.

                                  27          As a preliminary matter, the Court recognizes that while the question of DUTSA

                                  28   preemption is often fact-bound, courts applying Delaware law have nonetheless routinely
                                                                                         10
                                        Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST          Document 38       Filed 09/24/25      Page 11 of 14




                                   1   addressed it at the motion to dismiss stage. See, e.g., Battaglia Mgmt., Inc. v. Abramowicz, No.

                                   2   23-cv-615-GBW, 2024 WL 3183063, at *5 (D. Del. June 26, 2024) (collecting cases); but see

                                   3   Accenture Glob. Servs. GMBH v. Guidewire Software Inc., 631 F. Supp. 2d 504, 508 (D. Del.

                                   4   2009) (“Whether a party has, in fact, ‘grounded’ a common law claim ‘in the same facts’ as its

                                   5   trade secret claim often cannot be determined at the motion to dismiss stage.”). Relatedly, Rule

                                   6   8’s general allowance of alternative pleading does not apply in the DUTSA preemption context.

                                   7   See Savor, Inc. v. FMR Corp., 812 A.2d 894, 898 (Del. 2002) (rejecting petitioner’s argument that

                                   8   it should have been allowed to maintain its alternative common law claims in the event that its

                                   9   statutory trade secret claims were dismissed given DUTSA’s express objective to displace

                                  10   common law claims based on misappropriation).

                                  11          Turning to Panacea’s claims, the Court finds that DUTSA preempts its state law claims for

                                  12   unjust enrichment and common law misappropriation. Tallied cites several cases in which courts
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   have found that DUTSA preempts those claims under similar circumstances. See ECF No. 28 at

                                  14   20 (citing 250ok, Inc. v. Message Sys., Inc., 2021 WL 225874, at *1 (Del. Ch. Jan. 22, 2021);

                                  15   Alarm.com Holdings, Inc. v. ABS Cap. Partners, Inc., 2018 WL 3006118, at *10 (Del. Ch. June

                                  16   15, 2018), aff’d, 204 A.3d 113 (Del. 2019); Cal. Safe Soil, LLC v. KDC Agribusiness, LLC, 2025

                                  17   WL 98479, at *24 (Del. Ch. Jan. 10, 2025)). While Panacea argues that these cases are

                                  18   distinguishable, it merely recites the preemption standard that “the common law causes of action

                                  19   alleged by Panacea are not ‘grounded in the same facts’ as the DUTSA claim” without explaining

                                  20   how that is true or what separate facts its common law causes of action are grounded in. See ECF

                                  21   No. 29 at 19.

                                  22          Indeed, there is little daylight in Panacea’s complaint between its DUTSA trade secret

                                  23   claim and its claims of unjust enrichment and common law misappropriation. For unjust

                                  24   enrichment, Panacea alleges that “Tallied has benefited and been unjustly enriched by virtue of its

                                  25   wrongful and unlawful conduct, including its use of Panacea’s Confidential Information to (1)

                                  26   obtain the ADA RFP and (2) undermine and undercut Panacea’s ability to win the RFP.” ECF No.

                                  27   1 ¶ 86. In other words, Panacea alleges that Tallied has unjustly benefitted from misappropriating

                                  28   Panacea’s confidential information—the most pertinent of which involves the trade secrets alleged
                                                                                       11
                                        Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST           Document 38        Filed 09/24/25      Page 12 of 14




                                   1   here. See id. ¶¶ 91 (alleging that Tallied is liable for violating DUTSA by “unlawfully converting

                                   2   and using Panacea’s Confidential Information, . . . for its own purposes and with utter disregard

                                   3   for the effect of such disclosure on Panacea”). The same is true for Panacea’s common law

                                   4   misappropriation and/or conversion of confidential information claim—as the complaint repeats

                                   5   the exact language as for the DUTSA claim. Compare id. ¶¶ 90–91 with id. ¶¶ 96–97; see also

                                   6   Alarm.com Holdings, Inc., 2018 WL 3006118, at *11 (“Alarm has asserted a claim for common

                                   7   law misappropriation of confidential information, which to my mind is the clearest possible

                                   8   candidate for preemption under DUTSA.”).

                                   9          The Court, however, declines to find that Panacea’s claims for unfair competition and

                                  10   tortious interference with prospective business relationships are preempted at this stage. Unlike

                                  11   with the claims discussed above, Panacea has stated sufficient independent facts supporting its

                                  12   claims of unfair competition and tortious interference. Under Delaware law, “[b]oth claims
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   require a wrongful interference with the plaintiff’s expectancy in a business relationship that had a

                                  14   reasonable probability of being consummated.” You Map, Inc. v. Snap Inc., No. CV 20-00162-

                                  15   CFC, 2021 WL 106498, at *8 (D. Del. Jan. 12, 2021), report and recommendation adopted, No.

                                  16   CV 20-162-CFC, 2021 WL 327388 (D. Del. Feb. 1, 2021). The complaint alleges that Tallied

                                  17   feigned interest in entering into a partnership with Panacea to induce Panacea to disclose its

                                  18   confidential information about the ADA and the ADA’s RFP and ultimately used “dishonest,

                                  19   unfair, and improper means to interfere with [Panacea’s] prospective business relationship” with

                                  20   the ADA. See ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 103–04, 108. Those allegations are separate enough from the alleged

                                  21   misappropriation for these two claims to survive preemption at this stage. See Ethypharm S.A.

                                  22   France, 388 F. Supp. 2d at 435 (declining to find that DUTSA preempted a tortious interference

                                  23   with prospective business relationships because even “if the theft of the information does not rise

                                  24   to the level of misappropriation of trade secrets,” the intentional acts of using sensitive

                                  25   information to knowingly interfere with existing business relationships could be sufficient to

                                  26   satisfy the elements of the intentional interference claim).

                                  27          Accordingly, the Court grants Tallied’s motion to dismiss Panacea’s claims for unjust

                                  28   enrichment and common law misappropriation/conversion of confidential information, and it
                                                                                         12
                                        Case 4:25-cv-03194-JST           Document 38         Filed 09/24/25   Page 13 of 14




                                   1   denies the motion to dismiss the claims for unfair competition and tortious interference with

                                   2   prospective business relationships.

                                   3          C.      Breach of Contract

                                   4          Tallied largely repeats the arguments it made regarding the DUTSA claim for why Panacea

                                   5   has also failed to state a claim for breach of contract.

                                   6          First, Tallied argues that the information about the ADA RFP was not subject to the

                                   7   MNDA because “according to Panacea’s own allegations, for Tallied to have participated in the

                                   8   ADA RFP, Tallied must have received the RFP independently”—thus making the information

                                   9   about the RFP no longer confidential under the terms of the MNDA. ECF No. 28 at 22. As the

                                  10   Court explained above, even considering Tallied’s disputes of fact, Tallied’s argument only goes

                                  11   to whether knowledge of the actual RFP and scope of the RFP are confidential. The fact that

                                  12   Tallied may have ultimately learned about the ADA RFP on its own—after the ADA actually
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   issued its RFP—does not affect whether information shared regarding Panacea’s pricing strategy

                                  14   or ADA’s private preferences is confidential.

                                  15          Second, Tallied argues that Panacea has not provided sufficient factual detail to support its

                                  16   assertion that Tallied used Panacea’s information for its RFP bid and that Panacea’s claim that

                                  17   Tallied used any such information is entirely speculative. ECF No. 28 at 22. For the same reasons

                                  18   discussed above regarding misappropriation, the Court rejects Tallied’s argument and finds that

                                  19   Panacea has adequately alleged that Tallied used the confidential information disclosed under the

                                  20   MNDA to win the ADA RFP.

                                  21          Accordingly, the Court denies Tallied’s motion to dismiss Panacea’s claim for breach of

                                  22   contract.

                                  23                                              CONCLUSION

                                  24          For the foregoing reasons, the Court grants Tallied’s motion to dismiss in part and denies it

                                  25   in part. Panacea’s claims for unjust enrichment and common law misappropriation/conversion of

                                  26   confidential information are denied with leave to amend. The Court denies the remainder of

                                  27   Tallied’s motion.

                                  28   ///

                                   2   deficiencies identified in this order. The case management conference scheduled for October 7,

                                   4          IT IS SO ORDERED.
